records.name: Sud
records.summary:
The state's principal international LGBT-rights federation's annual country review (February 2025) finds a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people, with incidents reported almost monthly - and includes in that finding a March 2025 scooter-mounted homophobic assault on a young man in this region's largest metropolitan periphery.

In October 2025 at a commuter railway station in the region's main metropolitan area an activist - president of a local LGBT association - was subjected to an escalating verbal homophobic attack ending in threats of stabbing by two young men. The station setting is one any visitor could occupy. The underlying local-newspaper report was bot-blocked at fetch time; it is retained as a sourced event on the strength of the recorded claim.

sources.summary: International LGBT federation's annual country review for Italy (February 2025): finds a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people in 2024, incidents reported almost monthly, including the March 2025 scooter-mounted assault of a young man in Scampia (Naples).

Il Gazzettino (13 Oct 2025): Torre Annunziata — a 63-year-old man arrested after stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; a grave homophobic episode in the province of Naples, giving this record its region-specific violence datapoint.

records.name: Isole
records.summary:
At roughly 5 a.m. on 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten in a fast-food restaurant in this region's largest city solely because they were gay; the victims were hospitalised, video of the attack later circulated publicly, and the prosecutor's office reconstructed the sequence - insults and threats first, then the physical assault.

A June 2026 press survey of reporting from the region documents a sustained pattern rather than isolated events: rising homophobic bullying, violence against LGBTIA+ people and associated suicides, with multiple cases listed. The pattern is qualitative but official: a hospitalisation-level public assault and a prosecutorial reconstruction sit alongside a growing documented toll.

sources.summary: TG LA7: 26 April 2025, a fast-food restaurant in Catania — three young men beaten because they were gay; the prosecutor's office (Procura etnea) reconstructed the sequence of insults and threats before the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly.

Catania-based outlet (5 June 2026): 'Omofobia in Sicilia, continuano le violenze' — a 2026 follow-up cataloguing continuing assaults and suicide cases across Sicilian towns, the record's evidence that the 2025 pattern has not stopped.

records.name: Alberta
records.summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.

sources.summary: CBC (4 Dec 2024): Alberta's trio of trans-youth bills passed final legislative stage — the Education Amendment Act 2024 (parental opt-in for classroom instruction, student pronoun and sport rules), a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, plus sports policy. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

CBC (Dec 2024): Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting, invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years; Egale Canada, Skipping Stone Foundation and five families said their court challenge to Bill 26 continues regardless. Result: laws in force, constitutional litigation pending.

records.name: Saskatchewan
records.summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

sources.summary: Government of Saskatchewan education-ministry news release (22 Aug 2023) announcing the parental inclusion and consent policies: schools must seek parent/guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.
